extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy of language
extracted.subtask_description: Classification and analysis of names and propositions: their form, varieties, import, and how to determine what a proposition asserts (copula, modality, quantity, distribution, hypothetical vs categorical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of minds grounded on states of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Every attribute of a mind consists either in being itself affected in a certain way, or affecting other minds in a certain way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When we say a mind is 'devout' or 'cheerful' we mean that the ideas, emotions, or volitions implied form a frequently recurring part of that mind’s series of feelings; attributes can also be ascribed because the contemplation of a mind excites certain feelings in other minds (e.g., approbation). Example: 'generosity' asserts both a habitual state of mind and that the idea of those feelings excites approbation in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of bodies grounded on feelings they excite
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes may be ascribed to bodies on the ground of the feelings which they excite in other minds (e.g., the beauty of a statue is grounded on the pleasure it produces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such attributes are not solely grounded on sensation; emotions (pleasure, admiration) produced by contemplating the object can justify ascribing attributes like 'beauty'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Namable Things (four classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: All Namable Things can be classified as: (1) Feelings or States of Consciousness; (2) Minds which experience those feelings; (3) Bodies or external objects which excite certain of those feelings (and their powers/properties); (4) Successions and Co-existences, Likenesses and Unlikenesses between feelings or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumeration is offered as a substitute for Aristotelian Categories and is intended to serve as the basis for analyzing the import of propositions and what the mind actually believes when assenting to a proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between psychological (subjective) and objective facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every fact solely composed of feelings or states of consciousness is a Psychological or Subjective fact; every fact composed wholly or in part of substances and attributes is called an Objective fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An objective fact is grounded on a corresponding subjective one and has no meaning apart from the subjective fact which corresponds to it, except as a name for the unknown process by which that subjective fact is brought to pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is a portion of discourse in which a predicate is affirmed or denied of a subject; a copula (sign of predication) is necessary to indicate this intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copula often takes the form 'is' or 'is not'; inflection of verbs can also signal predication. It is important not to confuse the copula's function as a sign of predication with a claim of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copula is a sign of predication, not necessarily existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula indicates predication (affirmation or denial) and does not necessarily imply the existence of the subject (e.g., 'A centaur is a fiction of the poets' does not assert existence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of the ambiguity of 'to be' — it functions both as a copula and as an existential predicate; conflating these leads to metaphysical confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative vs Negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions divide into affirmative (predicate affirmed of subject) and negative (predicate denied of subject); the copula expresses affirmation ('is') or negation ('is not').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some logicians attempt to treat negation as part of the predicate (affirming a negative name), but this obscures the real distinction between asserting a fact and asserting the non-existence of that fact; the negative form conveys absence, not presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality and tense attach to the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of tense or modality (past, present, future; may, perhaps, possible) properly belong to the copula, since they modify the predication itself rather than the subject or predicate alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat temporal and modal qualifications as modifications of the sign of predication because they affect the applicability of the predicate to the subject as expressed by the proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (singular) vs Compound (complex) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple proposition affirms or denies one predicate of one subject; a compound proposition contains more than one predicate or subject (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many so-called complex propositions are really aggregates of distinct propositions joined by particles ('and', 'but'). Some compound forms (disjunctive, conditional) are single assertions about relations between propositions rather than mere aggregations of simples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and analysis of hypothetical/conditional and disjunctive propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical (conditional) propositions assert an inferribility relation between propositions (the subject and predicate of such a proposition are themselves names of propositions); disjunctive propositions ('either...or') are equivalent to conditionals and can be resolved into conditional forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that in a conditional the subject is a proposition and the predicate is a general relative name applicable to propositions; the assertion is about inference, not direct predication of simple terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical vs hypothetical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical propositions assert without condition; hypothetical (conditional) propositions assert an inferential relation between propositions (i.e., that one proposition is a legitimate inference from another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the subject and predicate of a conditional proposition are names of propositions, and that this alters how we interpret what is being asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal, Particular, Indefinite, and Singular propositions (quantity of assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification based on generality of subject: Universal (predicate affirmed/denied of all individuals denoted by subject, e.g., 'All men are mortal'), Particular (of some portion, e.g., 'Some men are wise'), Indefinite (form unclear whether universal or particular), Singular (subject is an individual name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When context or convention does not supply whether a general name is intended universally or particularly, the expression is ambiguous; in practice context often determines the intended quantity (e.g., 'Man is mortal' normally understood universally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is distributed when it stands for each and every individual which it denotes. In 'All men are mortal' the subject 'men' is distributed; in 'Some men are mortal' it is undistributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distribution to concisely characterize universal vs particular propositions: a universal proposition is one of which the subject is distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions concern things themselves, not merely ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The import of a proposition is not the relation between the corresponding ideas in the mind but the assertion about the things themselves (external phenomena); propositions express facts about outward things, though mental ideas are conditions for forming belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing the import or truth of a proposition, focus on the external fact it refers to rather than reducing it to a relation between ideas—confusing the two has led to serious errors in the philosophy of logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes’s criterion of truth as name-coextensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's theory: in every proposition what is signified is the belief of the speaker that the predicate is a name of the same thing of which the subject is a name; if it really is so, the proposition is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures a necessary property of true propositions (coextensiveness of subject and predicate reference), illustrated by examples: 'All men are living beings' (true because 'living being' names what 'man' names) vs 'All men are six feet high' (false because 'six feet high' is not a name of every man).
